01_cold_open.text: [whispering, tense] It's two a.m. [pause] Why is my heart going this fast?
01_cold_open.speaker: YOU

01_cold_open.text: [faster, anxious] I have the meeting. And the rent. And I didn't answer her text. And—
01_cold_open.speaker: YOU

01_cold_open.text: [softly, cutting in gently] Hey. Hey. You know this feeling.
01_cold_open.speaker: NARRATOR

01_cold_open.text: Everyone does. Tight chest. Racing thoughts. That hum under everything.
01_cold_open.speaker: NARRATOR

01_cold_open.text: We even have one word for it.
01_cold_open.speaker: NARRATOR

01_cold_open.text: Here's the strange part. A hundred years ago, if you'd told most doctors you were "stressed"... they'd have pictured a bridge.
01_cold_open.speaker: NARRATOR

01_cold_open.text: Not a person. "Stress" was an engineering word. The load on a steel beam. The strain on a cable. [pause] Then one clumsy young scientist borrowed it... and gave it to all of us.
01_cold_open.speaker: NARRATOR

01_cold_open.text: And somebody paid for him to keep saying it.
01_cold_open.speaker: NARRATOR

01_cold_open.text: [beat] This is the story of the man who invented stress. And why, the way you were taught about it... might be part of the problem.
01_cold_open.speaker: NARRATOR

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: Montreal. The 1930s. A young researcher at McGill University named Hans Selye is hunting for something that would make his name. A brand-new hormone.
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: NARRATOR

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: [eager, muttering to himself] If I inject the extract... and the rats change... it's something new. It must be something new.
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: SELYE

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: Every day, he injects his rats with extract from cow ovaries. And, as the story is usually told... [amused] he's terrible at it.
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: NARRATOR

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: [offended] I am not terrible, I am— [gasps] No, no, no, no—!
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: SELYE

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: [laughing] He fumbles the injections. He drops the rats. They escape.
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: NARRATOR

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: [breathless, chasing, panicked] Come back—! Come back here—!
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: SELYE

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: And Hans Selye ends up chasing them around the lab... with a broom.
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: NARRATOR

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: [laughs] A broom?
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: YOU

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: [laughs softly] A broom. Months of this.
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: NARRATOR

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: Then he opens the rats up. And there it is. Swollen adrenal glands. A shrunken immune system. Bleeding ulcers in the stomach.
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: NARRATOR

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: [hushed, thrilled] It worked.
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: SELYE

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: He'd found his hormone. [pause] Except... he hadn't.
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: NARRATOR

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: Because he also had a control group. Rats he'd injected with nothing but salt water. Harmless.
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: NARRATOR

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: And they had the exact same damage.
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: NARRATOR

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: [quietly] Wait. The salt water ones too?
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: YOU

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: [quiet, deflated] ...That's not possible.
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: SELYE

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: It wasn't the extract. It wasn't anything he injected. What every rat had in common... was the experience. The needles. The dropping. The chasing. The broom.
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: NARRATOR

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: [slower] Their bodies weren't reacting to a chemical. They were reacting to... life going badly.
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: NARRATOR

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: So he tested it.
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: NARRATOR

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: [scribbling notes, muttering, faster each time] Cold... same. Exhaustion... same. Injury... [stunned] ...same.
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: SELYE

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: Different ordeals. Same response, every time.
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: NARRATOR

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: In 1936, he published it, a short letter in the journal Nature. It didn't even use the word "stress" yet. That came later.
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: NARRATOR

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: But when it came, Selye reached for the engineering word. Pressure on a structure. Load on a frame.
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: NARRATOR

02_act1_clumsy_scientist.text: And he spent the rest of his life carrying it around the world.
02_act1_clumsy_scientist.speaker: NARRATOR

03_act2_word_takes_over.text: By the 1950s, "stress" was everywhere. Magazines. Medical journals. Kitchen tables.
03_act2_word_takes_over.speaker: NARRATOR

03_act2_word_takes_over.text: [laughs softly] Not quite. Selye gave us a word for something real. Your body really does respond to pressure. That part was a genuine discovery.
03_act2_word_takes_over.speaker: NARRATOR

03_act2_word_takes_over.text: But a word that powerful... is useful to people. And not only to scientists.
03_act2_word_takes_over.speaker: NARRATOR

04_act3_waiting_room.text: San Francisco. The 1950s. Two heart doctors, Meyer Friedman and Ray Rosenman, have a waiting room problem.
04_act3_waiting_room.speaker: NARRATOR

04_act3_waiting_room.text: Their chairs need fixing. So they call in an upholsterer.
04_act3_waiting_room.speaker: NARRATOR

04_act3_waiting_room.text: [looking the chairs over, puzzled] Huh. [beat] What kind of patients do you got in here, doc?
04_act3_waiting_room.speaker: UPHOLSTERER

04_act3_waiting_room.text: [busy, clipped, not looking up] Heart patients. Why?
04_act3_waiting_room.speaker: FRIEDMAN

04_act3_waiting_room.text: [matter-of-fact] 'Cause they only wear out the front of the seat. [taps the chair] Look. Nobody in here ever sits back.
04_act3_waiting_room.speaker: UPHOLSTERER

04_act3_waiting_room.text: [small laugh] ...That's me in every waiting room.
04_act3_waiting_room.speaker: YOU

04_act3_waiting_room.text: Nobody sat back. They perched. On the edge. Ready to spring up.
04_act3_waiting_room.speaker: NARRATOR

04_act3_waiting_room.text: As Friedman later told the story, that was the moment it clicked. Maybe the people getting heart disease... had something in common.
04_act3_waiting_room.speaker: NARRATOR

04_act3_waiting_room.text: Always on the edge of the seat.
04_act3_waiting_room.speaker: NARRATOR

04_act3_waiting_room.text: They gave it a name you've definitely heard.
04_act3_waiting_room.speaker: NARRATOR

04_act3_waiting_room.text: And for a while... it looked like a breakthrough.
04_act3_waiting_room.speaker: NARRATOR

05_act4_who_paid.text: [darker, lower] Now. Think about who loves the idea that heart disease comes from your personality... and your stress.
05_act4_who_paid.speaker: NARRATOR

05_act4_who_paid.text: [bright, polished, too smooth] Tense? Wound up? Long day at the office? [beat] Take a moment. Light up. Relax.
05_act4_who_paid.speaker: AD VOICE

05_act4_who_paid.text: Decades later, researchers dug through millions of pages of tobacco industry documents. And they found something.
05_act4_who_paid.speaker: NARRATOR

05_act4_who_paid.text: In 1958, Hans Selye, the father of stress, wrote to a tobacco company asking for money.
05_act4_who_paid.speaker: NARRATOR

05_act4_who_paid.text: He got it. A lot of it. Over the years, the industry funded his work, and it used stress research in court, to argue that something else was making people sick.
05_act4_who_paid.speaker: NARRATOR

05_act4_who_paid.text: He didn't publicly declare those ties.
05_act4_who_paid.speaker: NARRATOR

05_act4_who_paid.text: And Type A? A later study found the tobacco industry had been a major funder of that research too.
05_act4_who_paid.speaker: NARRATOR

05_act4_who_paid.text: [quiet, stunned] ...So the cigarette companies helped sell me my stress.
05_act4_who_paid.speaker: YOU

05_act4_who_paid.text: [distant, fading, like a memory] ...Light up. Relax.
05_act4_who_paid.speaker: AD VOICE

05_act4_who_paid.text: [gently] They helped sell you a story about it. That stress is a thing that happens to you. A thing that breaks you. And that you need something to take the edge off.
05_act4_who_paid.speaker: NARRATOR

05_act4_who_paid.text: [pause] And that story might be doing more harm than the stress itself.
05_act4_who_paid.speaker: NARRATOR

06_act5_twist.text: In 2012, researchers looked at data on nearly thirty thousand American adults. They'd been asked two simple questions.
06_act5_twist.speaker: NARRATOR

06_act5_twist.text: How much stress do you have?
06_act5_twist.speaker: NARRATOR

06_act5_twist.text: And do you believe stress is hurting your health?
06_act5_twist.speaker: NARRATOR

06_act5_twist.text: Then the researchers waited, and looked at who had died over the following years.
06_act5_twist.speaker: NARRATOR

06_act5_twist.text: The people with a lot of stress, who believed it was harming them... had a 43 percent higher risk of dying early.
06_act5_twist.speaker: NARRATOR

06_act5_twist.text: [warmer, leaning in] But here's what nobody expected. People with just as much stress... who didn't see it as harmful... didn't show that risk at all. In fact, they had some of the lowest risk in the whole study.
06_act5_twist.speaker: NARRATOR

06_act5_twist.text: [slow] Same pressure. Different story. Different outcome.
06_act5_twist.speaker: NARRATOR

06_act5_twist.text: It's one study. It can't prove the belief itself caused it. But it raises a question worth sitting with.
06_act5_twist.speaker: NARRATOR

06_act5_twist.text: What if part of what hurts us... is the way we were taught to see it?
06_act5_twist.speaker: NARRATOR

07_ending.text: Hans Selye's rats got sick because their lives were being turned upside down by a clumsy man with a broom. That's real. Pressure is real.
07_ending.speaker: NARRATOR

07_ending.text: But think about what your body actually does.
07_ending.speaker: NARRATOR

07_ending.text: Your heart speeds up to send you more energy.
07_ending.speaker: NARRATOR

07_ending.text: Your breathing quickens to bring in more air.
07_ending.speaker: NARRATOR

07_ending.text: [warmly] That's not a body breaking down.
07_ending.speaker: NARRATOR

07_ending.text: [quiet, slower now] It's two a.m. [breath] My heart's still going fast.
07_ending.speaker: YOU

07_ending.text: [a small, tired smile in the voice] ...Okay. [beat] Okay. I'm getting ready.
07_ending.speaker: YOU

07_ending.text: [softly] The word was invented. [pause] What you do with it... is still up to you.
07_ending.speaker: NARRATOR
